subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with "a number of" + plural noun crossed with present perfect versus past progressive decided by a present-tense consequence in the next sentence
passage: Keeping a rice paddy flooded all season starves its soil of oxygen, and microbes in the airless mud give off methane as a result. A number of the delta's rice growers ______ by draining their fields between irrigations so that air can reach the mud. Their paddies emit markedly less methane than neighboring fields, and their harvests are no smaller.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "A number of the delta's rice growers." "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb, so the head word "number" does not make the subject singular; the verb must be plural, agreeing with "growers." The next sentence states the result in the present tense: "Their paddies emit markedly less methane" and "their harvests are no smaller." A past change whose consequence holds in the present calls for the present perfect, so the answer is "have adapted." "has adapted" has the right aspect but is singular, treating "number" as the subject. "were adapting" is plural but past progressive, describing an action in progress at some past moment that the passage never establishes, which does not fit the present-tense result. "was adapting" is both singular and past progressive.
topic_tag: rice agronomy: alternate wetting and drying

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural-form singular discipline name ("hydroponics") crossed with present versus past tense decided by the present-tense verbs of the surrounding sentences
passage: On desert farms near the coast, hydroponics ______ widely enough to supply lettuce and tomatoes to inland cities. Growing crops in nutrient solution instead of soil can cut irrigation water by up to ninety percent, because the roots take up only what they need and the rest flows back through the system. Growers on those farms add mineral salts to recirculating tanks and adjust the mixture as the plants mature.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "hydroponics," the name of a growing method; although it ends in -s, it is a singular noun, like "genetics," so the verb must be singular. The sentences that follow describe a current practice in the present tense: the method "can cut" water use, the rest "flows" back, and "Growers on those farms add mineral salts" and "adjust the mixture." The verb must therefore be present: "is practiced." "are practiced" is present but plural, treating the -s ending as a plural marker. "was practiced" is singular but past, which would place the farming in the past even though the last sentence says the growers on those same farms add salts today. "were practiced" is both plural and past.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural head and a reduced participial relative ending in a singular noun, crossed with active versus passive voice decided by the agent named in the first sentence
passage: Technicians at a regional blood bank test donated plasma for viruses before it can be given to a patient, sometimes repeatedly when an early result is unclear. Physicians will not release a unit until a final test resolves any doubt. The plasma units collected from one donor with an unusual antibody ______ four separate times, and each round of testing produced the same ambiguous reading.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "The plasma units," whose head noun "units" is plural; "collected from one donor with an unusual antibody" is a reduced relative clause that modifies "units," so the singular "donor" and "antibody" beside the blank do not control the verb. The verb must be plural. The first sentence names who does the testing: "Technicians at a regional blood bank test donated plasma," so the units are tested rather than doing any testing, and the verb must be passive: "have been screened." "have screened" is plural but active; it would say the units screened something, and "four separate times" is not an object. "has been screened" is passive but singular, agreeing with "antibody." "has screened" is both singular and active.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in the second half of a comparative correlative with a fronted plural object, crossed with simple present versus present perfect decided by the parallel present verb in the first half
passage: Producing nectar costs a plant sugar that it could otherwise spend on leaves and roots. In field plots of wild sunflowers, the reward appears to repay the expense: the more nectar the flower heads secrete, the more foraging bees a single plant ______. The most heavily visited plants go on to produce the heaviest flower heads by the end of summer.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: In the second half of the comparison, "the more foraging bees" is the fronted object and "a single plant" is the subject, so the verb must agree with the singular "plant," not with "bees." The two halves of a "the more ..., the more ..." comparison are parallel, and the first half uses the simple present: "the flower heads secrete"; the next sentence also uses the simple present: "The most heavily visited plants go on to produce." The verb must therefore be simple present and singular: "attracts." "attract" is simple present but plural, agreeing with the fronted "bees" or copying the plural "secrete." "has attracted" is singular but present perfect, which breaks the parallel with "secrete." "have attracted" is both plural and perfect.
topic_tag: plant reproductive ecology: sunflower nectar rewards

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural head whose restrictive object-relative clause carries its own singular subject and verb, crossed with present vs. past progressive decided by past-tense narrative verbs
passage: The piezometers that the night technician could reach without a boat ______ steadily higher readings each evening as the new reservoir filled behind the earthen dam. Alarmed by the trend, the engineers opened a line of relief wells along the downstream toe of the embankment, and within a week the water pressure inside the dam leveled off.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "piezometers"; "the night technician could reach without a boat" is a relative clause with its own singular subject, so neither "technician" nor "boat" controls the main verb, which must be plural. The passage narrates a finished episode in the past: the reservoir "filled," the engineers "opened" relief wells, and the pressure "leveled off," so the verb must be past: "were recording." "was recording" is past but singular, agreeing with "technician" or "boat" inside the relative clause. "are recording" is plural but present, which clashes with the past-tense account of what happened during the filling. "is recording" is both singular and present.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a singular head whose "between X and Y" modifier contains a compound, crossed with simple past passive vs. present perfect passive decided by a past-tense verb that closes the interval
passage: The alignment between the northern heading and the southern heading ______ every few days with laser surveys as two tunnel-boring machines advanced toward each other beneath the mountain. When the machines finally broke through, the two halves of the new water-supply tunnel met with an offset of less than two centimeters, a result that the project's surveyors celebrated.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "alignment"; "the northern heading and the southern heading" is a compound inside the prepositional phrase "between ...," not a compound subject, so the verb must be singular. The checking happened only while the machines "advanced toward each other," and the next sentence closes that period: the machines "broke through" and the halves "met," so the verb must be simple past: "was checked." "has been checked" is singular but present perfect, which wrongly ties a finished, closed-off period of surveying to the present. "were checked" is past but plural, treating the two headings as the subject. "have been checked" is both plural and present perfect.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement after "nor" with auxiliary inversion and a singular postposed subject, crossed with do-support vs. perfect auxiliary decided by the lexical base verb
passage: Hydrologists estimating how much water a mountain snowpack holds must combine two incomplete sources. The automated ground stations scattered across a typical watershed have never sampled more than a small fraction of its area, nor ______ newer, considerably more sensitive radar instrument aboard an orbiting satellite measure snow depth reliably beneath a dense forest canopy.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: After "nor," the auxiliary comes before the subject, and the subject here is "instrument," five words later, not the plural "stations" of the first clause, so the auxiliary must be singular. The main verb of this clause is the base form "measure," ten words after the blank, and a base form needs the auxiliary "do," not "have" (which would need "measured"): "does the." "do the" uses the right auxiliary but is plural, copying the number of "stations." "has the" is singular but takes the perfect auxiliary, which cannot combine with "measure." "have the" copies the first clause's "have never sampled" in both number and auxiliary.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with "the latter" resuming a plural noun from the previous sentence, crossed with simple past vs. present perfect decided by past-tense verbs anchoring a finished period
passage: Engineers building the first railways tried two kinds of track: short cast-iron rails and long wrought-iron rails. The latter, rolled in lengths of several yards, ______ per mile of track, but the brittle cast rails cracked under heavier locomotives, and by the end of that period every major line had replaced them.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "The latter" refers to the second of the two kinds of track named in the first sentence, "long wrought-iron rails," which is plural, so the verb must be plural even though "latter" looks like a single item. The passage describes a finished historical period: engineers "tried" both kinds, the cast rails "cracked," and every line "had replaced" them, so the verb must be simple past: "were costlier." "was costlier" is past but singular, treating "the latter" as one thing. "have been costlier" is plural but present perfect, which wrongly connects a closed episode in early railway history to the present. "has been costlier" is both singular and present perfect.
topic_tag: railway history: cast-iron versus wrought-iron rails

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a singular head separated from its verb by an interpolated comment clause with a plural subject, crossed with active vs. passive perfect decided by an object delayed by an interrupter
passage: A moon too small to retain much internal heat should, in theory, be frozen solid. One such icy moon, spacecraft measurements suggest, ______, through a set of long fractures near the pole, towering jets of water vapor and salty ice grains into space. Because the grains contain dissolved minerals, many planetary scientists infer that a liquid ocean lies beneath the frozen crust.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "moon"; "spacecraft measurements suggest" is a comment clause set off by commas, so its plural subject "measurements" does not control the main verb, which must be singular. After the interrupter "through a set of long fractures near the pole," the verb takes a direct object, "towering jets of water vapor and salty ice grains," so the moon is doing the ejecting and the verb must be active: "has been ejecting." "has been ejected" is singular but passive, which would make the moon itself the thing ejected and leave "towering jets" with no grammatical role. "have been ejecting" is active but plural, agreeing with "measurements." "have been ejected" is both plural and passive.
topic_tag: planetary science: cryovolcanic plumes on icy moons

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural possessor before a singular head noun (the [pl]' [sg]) crossed with present perfect versus simple present decided by a past-tense starting point and a present-tense continuing verb
passage: Two statisticians drafted the province's first household census in a single winter, arguing over nearly all of its questions. Even so, the statisticians' questionnaire ______ to regional planners and university demographers from the season it was printed, and analysts who design new surveys borrow its wording more often than that of any later form.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "questionnaire," a singular noun; "the statisticians'" is only a possessive describing whose questionnaire it is, so it cannot be the subject, and the verb must be singular. The verb must also be present perfect: the state began at a past point, "from the season it was printed," and still holds, as the present-tense "borrow" in the same sentence shows, so only "has been indispensable" spans that interval. "have been indispensable" has the right aspect but is plural, agreeing with the possessive "statisticians'." "is indispensable" is singular, but the simple present cannot reach back to a starting point in the past ("from the season it was printed"). "are indispensable" is both plural and in the wrong tense.
topic_tag: historical demography: a provincial census questionnaire

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement on the second verb of a compound predicate far from its plural subject, after a singular object, crossed with simple versus progressive present perfect decided by the first predicate and a later past-tense verb
passage: The diary records the lessons, quarrels, and harvests of a one-room school. Retired teachers who volunteer at the county museum transcribed the water-stained diary of its last schoolmistress and ______ to statewide registries of rural manuscripts. Both registries stopped accepting entries two winters ago, and historians who consult them treat both as closed collections.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The blank is the second verb of a compound predicate whose subject is "teachers," at the start of the sentence, so the verb must be plural; "schoolmistress," the singular noun just before "and," belongs to the first predicate ("transcribed the water-stained diary of its last schoolmistress") and is not a subject. The action must also be a completed one, not an ongoing one: it is paired with the simple, completed "transcribed," and the next sentence says the registries "stopped accepting entries two winters ago," so no contributing can still be in progress. Only "have contributed" is plural and completed. "have been contributing" is plural but describes an activity continuing up to now, which a registry that stopped accepting entries two winters ago rules out. "has contributed" is completed but singular, as if "schoolmistress" were the subject. "has been contributing" is both singular and progressive.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a whose-relative clause (singular antecedent, whose + plural noun as the clause subject) crossed with past versus present progressive passive decided by the past-tense frame verbs
passage: During the occupation, a single playwright kept the city's banned theater alive almost by herself. The playwright, whose unsigned scripts ______ hand to hand after dark, wrote under four invented names and never attended a performance of her own plays. Actors memorized each scene within a night and then burned the pages.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Inside the relative clause, the subject of the blank is "scripts" ("whose unsigned scripts"), which is plural; "playwright" is the subject of the main clause, whose verb is "wrote," not of the relative clause, so the verb must be plural. The verb must also be past: the frame is a past narrative, with "kept" in the first sentence, "wrote" and "never attended" in the playwright's own clause, and "memorized" and "burned" in the last sentence. Only "were being passed" is plural and past. "are being passed" is plural but present, which clashes with "wrote" and the rest of the past narrative. "was being passed" is past but singular, agreeing with "playwright." "is being passed" is both singular and present.
topic_tag: theater history: clandestine performance under occupation

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a nonrestrictive which-clause whose antecedent is the whole preceding clause, ending in a plural noun, crossed with simple present versus present perfect passive decided by the habitual present-tense frame
passage: Whenever a museum lends one of its panel paintings, a conservator first strips the yellowed varnish left by earlier owners, which ______ in written reports as a separate treatment. Registrars at the borrowing museum read that entry when the crate arrives and compare the panel's surface against it before the painting goes on view.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "which" here refers to the whole action of the preceding clause, the conservator's stripping of the varnish; that action is what can be recorded "as a separate treatment," whereas "owners," the plural noun just before the comma, cannot be a treatment. A clause used as an antecedent takes a singular verb. The verb must also be simple present: the sentence describes a routine that recurs "Whenever a museum lends" a painting, and the next sentence continues that routine in the present tense ("read," "compare," "goes"), so the logging is part of each repetition rather than a single completed event. Only "is logged" is singular and simple present. "has been logged" is singular but presents the logging as one finished event, which does not fit a procedure repeated whenever a painting is lent. "are logged" is simple present but plural, as if "owners" were the antecedent. "have been logged" is both plural and perfect.
